title: The Marquee Bill Lands Today. The Tax Bill Lands in May.
linkedin:
Melbourne Cup week fills marquees and corporate boxes across the East Coast. The invoice for that hospitality lands within days.

The tax bill it quietly creates doesn't.

Fringe Benefits Tax runs on its own year, 1 April to 31 March, separate from the income tax year most owners think in. Spend incurred during this week's Spring Carnival sits inside the FBT year that closes next 31 March, with the return typically lodged and paid around May.

That means the cash cost of today's client entertainment can land close to six months after the marquee has been packed down and the invoice reconciled. By the time the bill arrives, the Spring Carnival feels like old news and the budget line it came from has usually been closed off.

The pattern we see across owner-led businesses isn't a problem with the compliance work. Your BAS agent or accountant is doing exactly what they should with FBT, calculating it correctly once the year closes. The gap is that almost nobody treats the spend as a cash flow event in the moment it happens.

The fix is simple once it's named. Provision for the likely FBT cost at the time the spend occurs, using last year's return as a guide, and carry it as a held line in a rolling cash flow forecast rather than a loose mental note.

None of this is a case for spending less on clients this Spring Carnival. It's a case for looking six months past every entertainment invoice, not just at the invoice itself.
